samples.prompt: Some educators believe that the school day should be longer so children have more time to develop a wider range of skills. Others argue that a shorter school day allows children time for play, family, and independent interests. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
samples.modelAnswer:
Whether children benefit more from extended school hours or from a shorter, less structured day is a debate that touches on philosophies of education as much as on practical scheduling. There are reasonable arguments on each side, though I tend to favour the shorter day.

Those who advocate longer school hours point out that the modern curriculum is already crowded, and that extending the day would create space for music, sport, second languages and project-based work that timetables often squeeze out. Supporters add that working parents would benefit from reliable childcare, and that disadvantaged students in particular tend to make stronger gains when their educational hours match those of their wealthier peers, who often receive private tutoring after school.

However, the opposing argument is no less compelling. Children, especially younger ones, learn through unstructured play, social interaction with siblings and friends, and the freedom to follow their own curiosity. A longer school day risks producing cognitive fatigue and reducing the time available for the family conversations, hobbies and outdoor activity that contribute to balanced development. Several Nordic education systems have demonstrated that shorter, focused school hours can produce excellent outcomes when paired with high-quality teaching.

In my view, the question is less about hours than about what those hours contain. A long day of passive instruction adds little; a shorter day combined with rich opportunities for independent exploration outside school is preferable. In conclusion, while extra structured time has clear advantages for some learners, a shorter school day better serves the broader needs of childhood development.

(269 words)
commonMistakes: Sitting on the fence: 'both sides have merit' is not a position.
Listing too many unsupported arguments rather than developing two well.
Ignoring the question's specific framing (school day length, not school attendance).
improvementTips: Restate your position in the conclusion using different words than your introduction.
Use one concrete example per argument rather than two vague ones.

samples.prompt: Mobile phones have changed how families communicate, but not always for the better. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
samples.modelAnswer:
Mobile phones have undeniably transformed family life, making it easier to coordinate logistics and stay in touch across distances. Yet the impact on the quality of communication within the home is more mixed. On balance, I largely agree that phones have weakened the kind of conversation families used to share.

The most visible problem is the steady erosion of shared attention. Where family meals were once a forum for unhurried conversation, they are now often punctuated by glances at notifications, replies to messages and silent scrolling. When attention is divided in this way, conversations become shallower and less satisfying for everyone, even if no one consciously intends to be rude. Younger children, in particular, learn how to communicate by watching adults, and they absorb the lesson that the device usually wins.

It would, however, be unfair to ignore the genuine benefits phones provide. Grandparents living abroad can speak to grandchildren by video call. Teenagers who feel unable to discuss difficult subjects in person can reach out by text. Group chats allow extended families to stay loosely connected without the cost of regular reunions. These are not trivial gains.

Nevertheless, the convenience of digital contact does not fully compensate for the depth lost in everyday interaction. Families that protect 'phone-free' moments — meals, the school run, the hour before bed — generally report stronger bonds. In conclusion, while mobile phones have made family communication more frequent, they have arguably made it less meaningful, and households benefit from deliberately reclaiming time for genuine attention.

(254 words)
commonMistakes: Vague claims about phones 'destroying' communication without nuance.
Treating teenagers and grandparents as one homogeneous group.
Forgetting to define what 'better' communication actually means.
improvementTips: When using 'to what extent', signal it explicitly: 'largely agree', 'partially agree'.
Concede a counter-point honestly — this raises the perceived sophistication of your essay.

samples.prompt: Many cities are suffering from increasing levels of air pollution. What are the main causes of this problem, and what solutions could governments and individuals adopt?
samples.modelAnswer:
Across the world, urban air quality has deteriorated to a point where it threatens both public health and economic productivity. Identifying the principal causes is straightforward; the harder question is what governments and individuals can realistically do.

The two dominant sources of urban air pollution are road transport and energy generation. Petrol and diesel vehicles release nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter directly into busy city streets, where pedestrians and cyclists inhale them at close range. Cities that still rely heavily on coal-fired power stations, or which sit downwind of industrial zones, suffer additional pollution from sulphur dioxide and heavy metals. Population density compounds these effects: in a city of millions, even small per-capita emissions add up to a serious public health hazard.

Governments have several effective tools at their disposal. Congestion charges and low-emission zones, of the kind introduced in London and Stockholm, have measurably reduced traffic-related pollution by pricing the cost of dirty vehicles into journeys. Investment in subsidised public transport and protected cycle networks makes alternatives genuinely attractive. On the supply side, accelerating the transition to a renewable electricity grid removes pollution at the source rather than trying to clean it up downstream.

Individuals also bear responsibility. Choosing walking, cycling or public transport when possible, sharing journeys, switching to electric vehicles where affordable, and reducing household energy waste all make incremental contributions. None of these actions is dramatic in isolation, but at the scale of a city, they matter.

In conclusion, air pollution is primarily caused by transport and energy use, and reducing it requires coordinated structural reform alongside changes in daily behaviour.

(269 words)
commonMistakes: Listing causes without explaining their mechanism.
Suggesting only vague solutions like 'people should be more aware'.
Neglecting the second part of a two-part question.
improvementTips: Cite a specific city or policy where possible — this raises the credibility of your essay.
Distinguish between supply-side solutions (fewer emissions at source) and demand-side solutions (fewer trips).

samples.prompt: More employees today are choosing to work flexible hours rather than the traditional nine-to-five schedule. Why is this happening, and is it a positive or negative development?
samples.modelAnswer:
The traditional nine-to-five working day, once the unquestioned norm, is steadily losing ground as more employees opt for flexible schedules. There are several drivers behind this shift, and on balance I view it as a positive development, though with important caveats.

Several factors explain the movement away from fixed hours. The pandemic forced many organisations to trust their staff to manage their own time, and that trust, once established, has proven difficult to revoke. Digital tools now make asynchronous collaboration genuinely effective, so colleagues no longer need to be at their desks at the same time to be productive. Beyond the workplace, families with two working parents find that staggered hours make childcare significantly more manageable. Knowledge workers in particular tend to be most productive during specific times of day that vary by individual, and flexible scheduling lets them work in alignment with their own circadian rhythms.

The positives of this development outweigh its drawbacks. Workers report higher job satisfaction, lower stress and better physical and mental health when they control their schedule. Employers benefit from reduced turnover and a wider talent pool, since flexibility is one of the most reliable retention tools available. Productivity often rises rather than falls, because employees are working when they are sharpest rather than when the clock dictates.

There are, however, legitimate concerns. Some workers struggle to switch off and end up working longer hours than before. Junior staff may receive less informal mentorship when colleagues are not visible. These risks can be managed, but they require thoughtful management rather than wishful thinking.

In conclusion, flexible working has emerged for good reasons and offers real benefits, provided organisations actively guard against its predictable downsides.

(280 words)
commonMistakes: Treating 'flexible hours' as synonymous with 'working from home'.
Ignoring the second part of the question (positive or negative).
Generalising from one industry's experience to the entire workforce.
improvementTips: Acknowledge both sides briefly even when taking a clear position — it shows critical thinking.
Use a phrase like 'on balance' or 'with important caveats' to signal nuance.

samples.prompt: Some people think that paying taxes is enough of a contribution to society. Others believe that citizens have additional responsibilities. To what extent do you agree?
samples.modelAnswer:
Paying taxes is undoubtedly one of the most concrete obligations citizens have to the society that sustains them. Yet to argue that it discharges all civic responsibility is, in my view, to take an impoverished view of what citizenship requires.

The argument that taxes are sufficient is not without merit. Tax revenue funds the schools, hospitals, roads, courts and welfare systems that hold modern societies together. Citizens who pay their taxes honestly, particularly those at higher income levels who contribute disproportionately, are doing more than many give them credit for. Asking them to also volunteer their time, attend community meetings or donate to charity can feel like an unfair second tax on people who are already doing their share.

However, a healthy society depends on far more than the services taxes can buy. Strong communities are built through participation: serving on a school governing board, voting in local elections, organising neighbourhood improvements, helping a vulnerable neighbour through a difficult winter. None of these can be outsourced to the state without significant loss. Civic engagement also acts as a check on government: well-informed citizens who actively participate in public debate make democratic systems more accountable and more resilient.

Furthermore, the tax-only view assumes a transactional relationship between citizen and state that is at odds with how trust and social cohesion actually develop. Societies in which citizens engage actively with one another tend to be safer, happier and more economically dynamic than those in which civic life is left to professionals.

In conclusion, while taxes are a necessary contribution, they are not a sufficient one; meaningful citizenship requires participation that goes beyond the tax return.

(279 words)
commonMistakes: Equating 'civic duty' purely with formal volunteering.
Treating taxation and engagement as competitors rather than complements.
Failing to define 'enough' before evaluating the claim.
improvementTips: Define key terms early to avoid arguing past the question.
Use a 'however' pivot to transition from the conceded view to your own.

samples.prompt: International tourism has grown rapidly over recent decades. Do the advantages of this growth outweigh the disadvantages for the host countries?
samples.modelAnswer:
International tourism has expanded into one of the largest industries on the planet, employing hundreds of millions of people and reshaping the economies of many host nations. Whether its advantages outweigh its drawbacks depends heavily on how it is managed, but in well-regulated contexts the balance is positive.

The benefits begin with the obvious economic ones. Tourist spending generates foreign exchange earnings, supports small businesses such as guesthouses, restaurants and tour operators, and creates jobs that often require limited formal training, making employment accessible to younger workers and those in rural regions. Tourism revenue can also be channelled into preserving historical sites and protecting natural environments that might otherwise be neglected.

The disadvantages, however, are real and increasingly visible. Cities such as Venice, Barcelona and Kyoto have seen residents priced out of their own neighbourhoods as housing is converted to short-term rentals. Crowds erode the quality of cultural sites and degrade fragile ecosystems. Local cultures risk being repackaged as performances for visitors, losing their authenticity in the process. The carbon cost of long-haul flights adds a further global dimension to what might otherwise look like a local trade.

Whether these advantages outweigh the disadvantages depends on the policies in place. Destinations that enforce caps on visitor numbers, tax short-term rentals, invest tourism revenue back into local services and promote shoulder-season travel typically capture the benefits while limiting the harms. Where regulation is weak, the calculation tips the other way.

In conclusion, tourism's growth offers significant economic and cultural opportunities, but realising them without unacceptable costs requires active management rather than passive welcome.

(265 words)
commonMistakes: Treating tourism as a single phenomenon rather than varying widely by type.
Citing only economic effects on both sides.
Concluding 'it depends' without explaining on what.
improvementTips: Name two or three real destinations to illustrate your arguments.
Use 'whether…depends on…' to frame nuanced positions clearly.

samples.prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students, while others argue that students should pay at least part of the cost. To what extent do you agree with one of these views?
samples.modelAnswer:
Few questions in education policy generate as much disagreement as how to fund universities. Some advocate fully free tuition, framing higher education as a public good; others argue that graduates should contribute to the cost of an education that visibly raises their lifetime earnings. I take the middle position: a substantial public subsidy combined with limited income-contingent payments from graduates is the most defensible approach.

The case for free university is compelling on grounds of social mobility. When fees are charged, even with loans available, students from less affluent backgrounds tend to make more risk-averse choices about whether to study and what to study. Countries that have maintained free or nearly-free tuition, such as Germany and Norway, have produced highly skilled workforces without obvious damage to fiscal sustainability. Universal access also reflects the reality that society benefits collectively from a more educated population through higher productivity, lower crime rates and stronger democratic participation.

However, the case for cost-sharing is not unprincipled. University graduates earn a measurable income premium over their lifetimes, and asking them to contribute a portion of that gain back to the public purse seems fair, particularly in countries where many people never attend university but still fund it through general taxation. Income-contingent loans, where repayments begin only after graduates reach a threshold income, address most equity concerns without removing the principle of personal contribution.

In conclusion, the strongest system combines generous public funding with modest, income-linked graduate contributions. Pure free tuition is fiscally fragile; pure full-cost fees are socially divisive. The middle path captures the best of each.

(272 words)
commonMistakes: Ignoring the question's invitation to take a side ('to what extent').
Confusing tuition costs with living costs.
Citing only one country's example as universal evidence.
improvementTips: If you take a middle position, state it clearly — don't hedge.
Use specific policy mechanisms (e.g. income-contingent loans) rather than vague calls for 'fairness'.

samples.prompt: Obesity rates among children have risen sharply in recent decades. What are the main causes of this trend, and what measures could schools and governments take to address it?
samples.modelAnswer:
Childhood obesity has risen to levels that public health authorities openly describe as a crisis. Understanding why this has happened, and what schools and governments can do about it, is essential if the trend is to be reversed.

The causes are interconnected. Cheap, ultra-processed food has displaced home-cooked meals in many households, and these foods are typically high in sugar, salt and refined fats while being unsatisfying enough that children eat more than they should. Sedentary patterns of life have grown alongside, with children spending hours on screens rather than playing outside or walking to school. Marketing aimed at children — both for sugary drinks and for snack products — actively shapes what children prefer, often without parents fully realising the influence at work.

Schools are in a strong position to act. Replacing vending machines with water fountains and fresh fruit, offering compulsory daily exercise, and embedding nutrition education in the regular curriculum all send consistent signals during the hours children spend on campus. Encouraging walking and cycling to school, where safe, restores active movement to daily routines.

Governments have more powerful levers still. Taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages have been shown to reduce consumption meaningfully in countries such as Mexico and the United Kingdom. Restricting the advertising of unhealthy products before nine in the evening protects children from sustained marketing pressure. Investing in safe cycling infrastructure and well-maintained public parks creates the environment in which active lifestyles become natural rather than effortful.

In conclusion, childhood obesity reflects a food and activity environment that has shifted against children's health, and reversing it requires coordinated action both inside the school gate and far beyond it.

(278 words)
commonMistakes: Blaming parents alone without examining the wider environment.
Suggesting purely educational solutions without addressing supply.
Listing causes that overlap heavily ('fast food' and 'unhealthy food').
improvementTips: Distinguish between supply-side measures (taxes, advertising) and demand-side measures (education, modelling).
Cite at least one country whose policy has produced measurable results.

samples.prompt: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to make decisions that affect people's lives — in healthcare, hiring, lending, and policing. To what extent should governments regulate these systems?
samples.modelAnswer:
Artificial intelligence is now embedded in a widening set of decisions that materially affect people's lives, from diagnosing illness to filtering job applications. I take the view that governments should regulate these systems firmly, though not so heavily that beneficial uses are stifled.

The case for regulation begins with the scale and opacity of these systems. Unlike a human decision-maker whose reasoning can be questioned, an algorithm may reject a loan application or flag a person for police attention without producing an explanation that the person affected, or even the operator, can follow. When the consequences are this significant — denied employment, denied credit, wrongful arrest — affected individuals deserve a meaningful right to contest the decision. They cannot do so without minimum standards of explainability and a clear audit trail.

Regulation also addresses the well-documented problem of biased training data. Systems trained on data that reflects historical discrimination tend to reproduce that discrimination at scale, sometimes amplifying it. Independent testing, statutory audit requirements and the right to human review in high-stakes settings are not optional refinements; they are the basic infrastructure of accountability.

There is a real risk, however, of over-regulation that stifles beneficial uses of the technology. Diagnostic AI in medicine, for example, has demonstrated genuine improvements in early cancer detection, and excessive compliance costs could deny those benefits to patients. Sensible regulation should therefore be proportionate to the level of risk: lighter touch for low-stakes applications, far stricter requirements where the consequences for individuals are severe.

In conclusion, the appropriate question is not whether to regulate AI but how. Calibrated, risk-based oversight preserves the benefits of the technology while addressing its serious and well-evidenced harms.

(283 words)
commonMistakes: Treating AI as a single uniform technology.
Citing science-fiction risks rather than concrete present-day harms.
Calling for regulation without specifying what kind.
improvementTips: Use the phrase 'risk-based' or 'proportionate' to signal nuance.
Mention a concrete domain (loans, hiring, healthcare) to anchor the abstract argument.

samples.prompt: Some people argue that governments should invest in expanding public transport in cities, while others believe more should be done to encourage private electric vehicles. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
samples.modelAnswer:
The transition to lower-carbon transport is one of the most consequential infrastructure decisions facing modern cities. Whether the priority should be public transport networks or private electric vehicles is hotly contested, and I lean firmly towards public transport.

Advocates of public transport investment point out that buses, trams and metros move people at a small fraction of the energy and street space required by private cars, regardless of what powers the cars. A single tram can carry the passengers of around two hundred cars; the difference in congestion, pollution and land use is enormous. Public transport is also socially inclusive: students, the elderly, people with disabilities and those who cannot afford private vehicles all gain mobility when systems are well funded and integrated.

The argument for prioritising electric vehicles is not without merit. They eliminate tailpipe emissions, which improves air quality immediately, and they suit suburban and rural areas where public transport is impractical. As electricity grids decarbonise, the lifetime emissions of electric cars continue to fall.

However, electric private vehicles do not solve the deeper problems of congestion, road danger, the space cost of parking, or the embodied emissions of building large numbers of new cars and replacing batteries every decade. They are a useful tool, particularly outside dense urban areas, but they cannot match the per-passenger efficiency of well-used transit.

In conclusion, while electric vehicles have a role to play in the broader transition, governments serious about both climate and quality of urban life should prioritise public transport. Cities work better when fewer people need to drive at all, not merely when those who drive do so in cleaner cars.

(278 words)
commonMistakes: Treating EVs as a complete solution to urban transport.
Ignoring rural and suburban differences from city centres.
Confusing tailpipe emissions with lifetime emissions.
improvementTips: Use a per-passenger or per-mile comparison to make efficiency arguments concrete.
Acknowledge geography — what works in central Tokyo may not work in rural Wyoming.

samples.prompt: Some people believe social media platforms should be legally required to remove harmful content within hours. Others argue that this creates risks for free expression. To what extent do you agree with strict removal rules?
samples.modelAnswer:
Whether social media platforms should be legally compelled to remove harmful content within strict time limits has become one of the defining policy debates of the digital era. I largely agree that some legal duty exists, but the simplistic 'remove within hours or face fines' framing creates more problems than it solves.

The argument for strict removal rules is straightforward. Some content — child sexual abuse material, terrorist recruitment, direct incitement to violence — is so harmful that any tolerance is unacceptable. For these categories, automated detection and fast removal save real lives, and platforms with the technical resources of Meta or TikTok have both the means and a clear moral duty to act. Without legal pressure, platforms have historically prioritised engagement metrics over harm reduction, and the social costs have been borne by the public rather than by the companies.

However, strict removal deadlines for broader categories of 'harmful' content carry serious risks. When platforms face large fines for under-removal but no comparable penalty for over-removal, they predictably take down anything ambiguous to be safe. The result is collateral censorship of journalism, satire, political speech and legitimate health information. Activists in authoritarian regimes who rely on these platforms to organise can find their accounts disabled by the same systems intended to protect them. Speed and accuracy are in tension; designing only for speed sacrifices the latter.

The better approach combines strict, narrowly defined categories where removal is mandatory with transparent appeals mechanisms, slower deliberation for borderline cases, and statutory transparency about what is being removed. In conclusion, regulation is justified but must be carefully designed to avoid replacing one harm with another.

(280 words)
commonMistakes: Treating 'harmful content' as a single category.
Ignoring the over-removal incentive that strict deadlines create.
Citing only Western platforms while making global claims.
improvementTips: Use the phrase 'collateral censorship' to capture the over-removal risk concisely.
Distinguish narrow categories where removal is clearly justified from broad categories where it is contested.

samples.prompt: Traditional skills and crafts are being lost in many countries as younger generations pursue modern careers. Why is this happening, and what can be done to preserve such skills?
samples.modelAnswer:
From handloom weaving to traditional carpentry, skills that took generations to refine are quietly disappearing in many parts of the world. Understanding why this is happening, and identifying what can realistically be done, matters because once these skills are lost, they are extremely difficult to reconstruct.

Several overlapping factors explain the decline. The most fundamental is economic: traditional crafts often produce items that cannot compete on price with factory-made alternatives, leaving practitioners with thin margins and uncertain income. Younger people, observing how hard their parents work for modest returns, understandably prefer salaried careers in cities. Urbanisation accelerates this by separating young people from the rural communities where many crafts were learned informally. Schooling, which is now nearly universal but rarely teaches local crafts, occupies the years in which apprenticeship would historically have taken place.

Reversing this decline requires action on the economic problem and the transmission problem in parallel. Economically, governments can support craft producers through fair-trade certification, subsidies for tools and training, and procurement preferences that channel public spending towards local artisans. Tourism boards in many countries have demonstrated that a well-presented traditional craft can become a genuine source of income rather than a charitable cause. On transmission, integrating local crafts into the school curriculum, funding paid apprenticeships, and documenting techniques in video and written form all help carry knowledge forward.

A further point is worth making: the goal should not be to freeze traditions in amber but to allow them to evolve. Crafts that adapt to contemporary uses, while maintaining their core skill base, tend to survive and even flourish.

In conclusion, traditional skills are declining for understandable economic and educational reasons, and preserving them requires both reliable income for practitioners and active transmission to the next generation.

(287 words)
commonMistakes: Romanticising tradition without addressing its economic reality.
Suggesting solutions that ignore practitioners' need to earn a living.
Treating culture as static rather than evolving.
improvementTips: Pair every cultural argument with an economic one.
Use the word 'evolve' rather than 'preserve' where appropriate — judges respond to nuance.

samples.prompt: More and more people are working for companies based in other countries, often without ever meeting their colleagues in person. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend?
samples.modelAnswer:
It has become increasingly common for skilled workers to be employed by companies based on the other side of the world, with colleagues they have never met face to face. This arrangement offers genuine advantages but also introduces real costs that organisations and individuals are still learning to manage.

The advantages start with opportunity. A talented developer in Lagos or Manila can now work for a firm in San Francisco or Berlin and earn an income far above local averages without leaving family or community behind. Companies, in turn, gain access to a global talent pool, allowing them to recruit specialists they could never have hired locally. Distributed teams that span time zones often deliver work around the clock, with overnight progress that would be impossible from a single office. Workers also retain the flexibility of remote arrangements, with no commute eating into their day.

The disadvantages are subtler but real. Informal communication — the small conversations that happen between meetings, in corridors and over coffee — is largely lost in distributed teams. New employees find it harder to learn the unwritten norms of an organisation when they cannot watch colleagues at work. Time-zone differences can shift the burden of awkward hours onto workers in particular regions, often those outside the company's home country. Cultural misunderstandings, when they arise, take longer to surface and resolve through video calls than through shared physical space.

In conclusion, working remotely for overseas employers offers significant opportunities for individuals and companies alike but also introduces challenges around communication, cohesion and equitable working hours. Both sides benefit from honest acknowledgement of the trade-offs and deliberate effort to mitigate them.

(273 words)
commonMistakes: Listing the same point as both an advantage and disadvantage without explaining why.
Ignoring time-zone burdens, which mostly fall on workers outside the company's HQ region.
Claiming there are 'no disadvantages' or 'only disadvantages'.
improvementTips: Mention specific patterns like 'time-zone burden' to demonstrate precise vocabulary.
Use the word 'trade-off' to signal a balanced evaluation.

samples.prompt: Some people argue that individual lifestyle changes have very little impact on climate change compared to corporate and government action. To what extent do you agree?
samples.modelAnswer:
It has become fashionable to argue that asking individuals to recycle, eat less meat or fly less is largely beside the point, because the real responsibility for climate change lies with corporations and governments. I partly agree, but I think this framing dangerously underestimates what individuals collectively can do.

There is genuine truth in the systemic view. A small number of large oil and gas companies are responsible for a disproportionate share of historical emissions, and decisions made by governments about electricity grids, transport infrastructure and industrial regulation move emissions in or out of the atmosphere on a scale that no single household can match. It is morally and analytically wrong to place all responsibility on consumers, particularly poorer ones, while wealthy producers and inadequate regulators continue largely unchanged.

However, the conclusion that individual action does not matter does not follow. Companies sell what people buy, and changes in consumer demand cascade rapidly upstream. The rise of plant-based food, the collapse in coal use for home heating, and the rapid adoption of electric vehicles all reflect millions of individual decisions that have shifted markets in ways top-down policy alone would have struggled to achieve. Individual actions also have a demonstration effect: they normalise lower-carbon choices and create the political conditions for stronger collective action.

Furthermore, governments are made up of voters. People who change their own lives are far more likely to demand serious climate policy from those they elect, and to accept the short-term costs that some climate measures involve. The distinction between 'individual' and 'systemic' is in this sense partly artificial.

In conclusion, while corporate and government action carry most of the weight, individual choices both contribute directly and shape the political space in which systemic change becomes possible.

(290 words)
commonMistakes: Treating individual and systemic action as a zero-sum choice.
Citing 'the 100 companies' statistic without explaining the consumers behind it.
Dismissing all individual action as 'virtue signalling'.
improvementTips: Use the phrase 'demonstration effect' to argue that small actions seed larger ones.
Acknowledge the systemic point honestly before showing where it is overstated.

samples.prompt: In many countries, young people find it increasingly difficult to afford their own home. Why is this happening, and what could governments do to address the problem?
samples.modelAnswer:
Across much of the world, home ownership has receded out of reach for many young adults, a generational shift with consequences for family formation, wealth distribution and political stability. Understanding the causes and identifying realistic policy responses is essential.

The root cause is straightforward: in most growing cities, the supply of homes has failed to keep pace with the number of households wishing to live there. Restrictive planning rules, often well-intentioned, have made it slow and expensive to build new housing where it is most needed. At the same time, low interest rates over a long period inflated asset prices generally, and property in particular, far faster than wages. The result is that the ratio of typical house prices to typical incomes has reached historic highs in many cities, while older homeowners — who bought before this run-up — have benefited substantially from the same trend that excluded their children.

Governments have several effective options. The most important is to enable significantly more housebuilding, particularly higher-density homes near jobs and public transport, by reforming planning rules and reducing the procedural cost of approval. Building social and affordable housing directly, as Vienna has done over many decades, also disciplines the wider market. On the demand side, tax reform can shift the incentive away from treating homes as financial investments rather than places to live. Support for first-time buyers — savings schemes, stamp duty exemptions — can help, though if introduced without supply reform, it tends to push prices up further.

In conclusion, the affordability crisis facing younger generations is fundamentally a problem of inadequate supply combined with distorted demand, and meaningful progress requires governments to act decisively on both.

(283 words)
commonMistakes: Blaming individual buyers or sellers rather than supply and demand dynamics.
Suggesting only demand-side fixes (subsidies) without supply reform.
Ignoring intergenerational fairness.
improvementTips: Use the phrase 'house price-to-income ratio' to add precision.
Mention at least one city or country whose policy is widely studied.
